blocks.x: We start off by telling that this is an interview with Josiah Fraser. This is Bill Russell and Ralph Collins interviewing Mr. Fraser. And the place is 2014 Onzaga, your home. Yes, sir. And the date is December 14th, I believe, isn't it?
Yes, yes.
Now, can you tell us when you were born? Give me your full name, too, if you have a middle name.
I don't have no middle name, though. You ready? You ready yet? Yeah, go ahead. Go ahead. You mean it started when I was born? Yes. February 23rd, 1904.
1904, yeah.
Your name is Josiah?
Josiah Fraser. How do you spell that? J-O-S-I-A-H.
How do you spell your nickname there, your little name?
Well, they generally call me C-I-E.
C-I-E.
C-I-E. Some say S-I-E, but they were always pronounced as C-I-E.
What's that? Is that sort of a French nickname?
Oh, yeah. Well, it's adopted through the Creole people, you know, as a nickname from the name. The word Josiah, you see, is adopted from the Creole. Originated, started from the school days, S-I-E.
You had it all your life?
All my life you can say, yeah. And, well, let's see, I first started playing.
Now, maybe before you start on that, can you tell us a little bit about your family? I know, of course, you're related to the Barnes and the Morarras.
Morarras, that's right.
I understand, I think, Milly Barnes told us that the Fraser is the main name of the whole family originally.
It is, it is. That's right, it is.
You can tell a little bit how they're related.

Related. Well, Milly Barnes and Paul Barnes, their mother was my father's sister. And John Morrell, Simon Morrell, Lawrence Morrell, Eddie Morrell, all musicians. Their mother was my father's sister from the Fraser.
Their mother was the Fraser. And the Barnes' mother was the Fraser.
Was the Fraser. That's right. Yes, that's how they began.
Did you have, did your father play?
My father played guitar years back in the old-own Seminard Parish. The old guitar player, but he left and his main occupation was mattress making, self-employed.
Same as Milly Barnes.
Same as Milly Barnes and mattress making. And I first started that when I was a young boy and pick up the drums through the old-time Grafianolas. My oldest brother was a drummer, Sam Fraser.
Is he still living?
He's still living.
Is he around town here?
He lives at 1717 Fostyle Street. Him and...
And down the Night Wall?
Down the Night Wall, that's right. 17... 17 Fostyle Street. Him and...
You start to interview him. Does he play anymore?
No, he don't. He gave music up for a great many years. We'd still like to talk to him for a while if he'd have time. Yeah, well, I'll contact him for y'all. He's a...
And you might tell about your other brothers, too. I know you're younger.

Yeah, well, I have another brother which died in 49. My name is Alec Fraser. He was a piano player. He started off... Dave Williams, the piano player now playing in the French quarters. And he started a cousin of mine who died, too, called Mitchell Fraser. That was my father's youngest brother, Michelle Fraser. He started him out of play. Then he made... He played a while. He died in 49, yeah. And Dave Williams' mother, which I know you know him, Dave. His mother is ours as two cousins.
Oh, that's right.
He's related.
He was in the band that you all had last year with Lawrence.

Lawrence went to Cincinnati, yeah. And... And... Let me see, that's a Fraser, too, because... His mother's father was my father's brother. His name was Rosamore John Fraser. Then... You want me to get in down to it when I first started playing? Yes. And then you can start...
How many brothers and sisters did your father have?

My father had two brothers, two sisters. Oh, two brothers and two sisters. Yeah, Michelle Fraser, John Fraser, and Catherine Fraser, and Jeanette Fraser. Jeanette Fraser was Lawrence and then my mother.
What was your father's name again?
Samson Franklin Fraser. Samson Franklin Fraser. And...
Was he the oldest of the family, or...?
No, he was the second oldest, my father. Rosamore John Fraser was the oldest brother. My father was the second oldest brother. And Michelle Fraser was the youngest brother.
And...
And... That was a fellow by the name of Mitchell Fraser, another old-time piano player. He died... I'd say about... It's close to ten years now. And... And... Well, me and me... Amelia Bond...
Your younger brother, you still have another young...

Yeah, Simon Fraser. Yeah, he's living with my second oldest sister, yeah. Yeah. I think it's in the 26th... No, the 2500 Dumaine Street. He was in... That's the one... He allowed him how to play the piano to, Simon Fraser, yeah. And... Let's see, we have... Like I first said, I started... Now, my oldest brother, and Paul Barberin, another old drummer, they all started by Amarico's Woodyard on North Ramport Street years ago. And Sam, he played with Kid René and part with Louis Armstrong, before Louis ever think about leaving the Orleans to go north. See, they play with the old-time bands around, yeah. And he's the one... In fact, I used to use his drums around the front to him, you know, the practice behind the old-time... They call it the... These... Self-winding Victrola's. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Back around in 1920, like that, 1919. Right after World War I. But before that, like I said, I used to practice around the room on sticks, you know, just beating on steps and all like that. And then following behind the old-time pianola players, pianos. You see, I used to practice on that. Then I went along and started playing with this... That time before, radio time, we used to have...give house parties with piano and drum.
Did you...when you took up drums, did you have any lessons? Did your father help you or any...

No, no, no one learned how to play the drums. And in later years, in later years when I was...first band we organized was Lawrence on banjo, Adam Morrell on the bass, which is Lawrence's brother, cousin of mine. He's still living.
You see the one that's still living?
Yes, the one's still living. And a fellow by the name of Bush Hall and Raymond Brown on trombone.
Well, I remember Lawrence used to talk about Bush Hall.
Bush Hall.
Is he any relation...
No, only friends of ours.
I mean any relation of the other halls like Edmund Hall and...

No, relations at all. Bush Hall. No, he had no relation at all. Let's see. We formed a...we first called the band the Golden Rule New Orleans Jazz Band, the Golden Rule Band. And we said we had Paul Bones, Eddie, Morrell, Lawrence Morrell, and we didn't have no piano during them days with the outfit. And later on, we formally made the band into the Young Tuxedo Band. Name it after Paul. That time it was called the Original Tuxedo Band with Bebe originally on trombone, which is the manager. And... Come right on through.
That's all right. Come on.
I'll leave this over there.
I'll leave this over there on tip on that. All right. That's all right. You can't hear it. You're talking about Bebe originally. Yeah, you know. And Papa Celestan.

Well, that time he used to...that we had the original Tuxedo Band. And then we used the title of the Young Tuxedo Band. Now that outfit consists of Dwight Newman on piano, and we had trained over to Paul Bent on trombone, Dennis Harris on saxophone and clarinet, Louis Contrell on saxophone and tenor sax and clarinet. And the regular rhythm section consists of White Newman piano, Lawrence Morale banjo, Eddie Morale bass, and myself drums. That was the regular rhythm. Eight pieces out.
What kind of a drum set did you get in the beginning?

The first drum I ever owned was a Ludwig. Ludwig drum. How big was the bass drum? The bass drum in them days was 14 by 28. I bought the bass drum separately from C.G. Kahn. At that time it was at 116, I believe, Crown of that street. And the snare drum I bought that separately by a mail order house called the Willis and Music People out of Chicago.
Was that a Kahn, I mean Ludwig too?

No, that was a Lita snare drum. Lita snare drum. That's the first, yeah, that was... The bass drum was from Sir Kahn and the Lita was a... I mean the snare drum I bought from the Willis and Music People was a Lita snare drum. And uh...
Can you tell us anything else about your outfit that you have? Cowbells, wood blocks?
Well during that time, yeah, we used four cowbells, one wood block, small size tum tum, and no sock stand, and one crash cymbal. And the side cymbal on the bass drum.
Oh, you had it fastened down there on the bass drum. On the side.

And overhead the foot pedals. Yeah. And the track overhead, it was fastened from the top of the bass, and you had a wooden foot pedal. About what year was that? Was that after the First World War or before? That was after World War I, right after World War. That's around in the year around 19 to 24.
Were those the ladies thing at that time?

Well that was considered the ladies, overhead swinging pedals. And the later years around, I swing over to, we used to call them them times, the floor pedals, was around 1927. When they first came out? I don't know what they hear to come out, but that's when I swing over to. I don't remember that good, but I went on the boat that first started, used to call it the Idlewild. Used to operate from Napoleon in the river, like a colored pageant of boats, you know, like the steamer, that time during the steamer capital. Well we operated that with the Young Tuxedo Band.
And had dances at night.
The dances at night, yeah. And sometimes Sundays excursions. That's when I swing over to, that was in the year 1927. And that's where we, I swing over to. I bought that from C.G. Conn.
When you first started, where did you play? What jobs did you get with the Young Tuxedo Band?

Well, Young Tuxedo Band used to play the New Orleans Country Club, Saturday nights, dinner dance, 8 to 12. The Boston Club, Canal Street, for carnival season parties, which was given to us from the original Tuxedo Band. Sometimes we played with them. We played at the Atenine, St. Charles and Playo. We played some dances over there. We played at the old time, a place they call it. At the time they called it the Spanish Folk Country Club, at the old Punch and Train Boulevard. It was known that there as the Jewish Country Club they did. We used to call it the old Spanish Folk Country Club. Oh, I see. Yeah, them days. But it still was the Jewish Country Club, but them days we called it the Spanish Folk Country Club.
Now, who was the leader of that band, the Young Tuxedo?
The Young Tuxedo Band, Bush Hall. Oh, Bush Hall was the leader?
Lawrence Morales was the manager.
Yeah. Bush Hall was the leader.
Remember how much you got paid and everything?

During them days, for an eight-piece band, they'll run you. At the rate of some of these society dances, your money is to run between six and seven dollars a man, almost. Now, when we played for the balls, like on Saturday nights, the top price was for six-piece hours, it's thirty-one dollars for the whole band. Five dollars a man for six-piece and a dollar over for the leader. It was considered not the union prices.
Did they have a union in those days or was it very active or strong?

No, the union wasn't so very active around in the early parts of the twenties. I think I first joined the union in 19…let's see, I went into 1928, something like that. When George Augustine and formerly old bass player, and I forget that other man used to play a band, Willie Bontem. Oh, yeah. I met him once. Yeah, Willie Bontem. We sat at the old St. Catherine Hall on Tulane Avenue, I believe in South Villiers, somewhere up in the neighborhood. Yeah, the old St. Catherine Hall. It's still there. It's still there, yeah. It's what he was the president. In later years, the headquarters move over to, after the junk hotel on us, they call it now LaSalle Street, where the old man, Tats, daddy was janitor over there, he was our recording financial secretary. We used to call him in them days. The old man, I'm trying to think of his name now. He used to play the peck horn, the door baritone, you know, in all the funeral bands. Like old man Barberang used to play, you know, the alto horn. Yeah. And then we had, from that band… Wasn't named the Alexanders, I guess. That was Alexanders, yeah. Yeah, old man. But we had a nickname we used to call him. That's Tats. His right name is, Tats playing side, his right name is Adolf Alexander, but they all called him Tats for nickname.
Yeah. Did his father have a nickname?

Yeah, that's what I'm trying to think now. His father's nickname used to call him, I can't think of a president name. But anyhow, he was, I was financial secretary of the local. And then we kept that organization until Bush died. Then Dwight Newman, the piano player, he took the band over. And then we first, the man we had to place, Bush Hall, was a fellow by the name of Albert Dominick, known as Don Alick. Oh, yeah. Don Albert, yeah. I think he's now living in El Paso, Texas. In later years he formed a big large dance, you know, dance band. He made some records too. Yeah, he called us Don Albert's Arbistry, but he's from New Orleans, used to live on Robinson and St. Anthony. But he was…
We must try to remember to talk to his father is still living here. He's still living here.
Ferdinand, I believe his name is Ferdinand. Yeah, old cigar maker. And I knew Danny Dominick in Chicago, right? Yeah, yeah, yeah.
His uncle. That's right. And you tell me, a sort of interruption about the Young Tuxedo Band today. Did that sort of grow out of your band or just… Well, I wouldn't know.

Did you stop using the name or what happened? We just stopped using it after the band, it scattered about, you see, the members scattered about because the Young Tuxedo Band of the day, that's considered a band. That's considered a brass band, isn't it? Yeah, that's what I wondered.
Did you ever play any parades or have a brass band with that group too?

I don't know. I played in different brass bands, but not with the Young Tuxedo. That's John Kazmi. I worked with every brass band around here, such as… The first man started me into brass band work was Ernest Rapania, the old drummer. Oh, yes. And that was… I was doing them same music in the 20s. And… But you played with him…
Did you play bass or snare drum? I played the snare drum.

And he played bass. He played the bass, Ernest Rapania. I heard he was very good, famous, I mean, bass bass. He was the famous you had around here. I heard he was the famous you had around here. I heard he was the famous you had around here.
and a lot of parade music, Ernest Rapania. We used to call him Trap for nickname.
Trap, okay.
Yeah, Trap, yeah. That was his nickname.
Because of his drum? Oh, no, with his name.

This name, I guess taken from the drums. He was a good drummer, you know. Old-time drummer, good one. And he nicknamed him with Trap. His right name was Ernest Rapania. And during them days, that band was, I think it was connected with Manuel Perez, Imperial Brass Band. Yeah, I played with that outfit.
But your young tuxedo then was just strictly a dance.
Dance band, yeah. Yeah, the original young tuxedo band was strictly a dance band.
Can you tell us any more about Ernest Rapania? We don't hear too much about him.

Well, Ernest Rapania was a drummer working every cabaret around New Orleans. He, right after World War I, he was a veteran of World War I, and right after all, he worked at a place for years who was known as the hummingbird, I believe, which is beyond Franklin, between Bionerville and Iberville, form of the old district. He worked there for many years.
Can you remember anything about his outfit, his drums and so on?

Well, I do know he had, in the line of a snare, he had, and it's still being used today, if I'm not mistaken by Alfred, was a duplex snare drum. Looked like it was all lumen, a duplex snare drum. Alfred Williams, you think? I think he still has it. I think he has a duplex. I forgot. Yeah, well, that used to be on the Strapanius drum.
He might have told us that. I forgot.

Yeah, because I'm sure Alfred had that drum. I used it several times in some parades in the lately years with Poissy Huffer. Yeah, I've seen that drum. Yeah, when I used to relief Alfred sometimes and he'd be feeling bad.
I didn't know they made aluminum drums that far back.
Yeah, it was a lumen snare drum. Now, I couldn't remember what sort of a bass drum on his head, but it was a regular, you know, a regular bass, wood shell bass drums, separated tensions.
Yeah, the two rods and something.

Yeah, yeah, separated tumscrew rods. And then the later years, I went in from, let's see, it was 28, when I was working, John Robichauds, he had another dance orchestra. We used to play it, locally work around, you know, country club the same way, evening dances, night dances. It was like the Young Tuxedo Band. And during that year of, 20, later part of 1928, I was the, Paul Barbaran, when Lloyd Contrell died, the old drummer, he died, Paul Barbaran went into P-Round's band and he played a while him and his fellow by the name of Walter Pichauds and they formed the Pelicans of Silvertone Orchestra, Gravy and Ramport. And it was, consisted of Walter Pichauds and Paul Barbaran and it was, let's see, he was playing the David Jones saxophone and Manuel Sayles guitar, banjo. I just remember all the men that present, but I mean it's, and then he was in P-Round's band and he left the band at 28th and I met some of P-Round's bands at the place they call the Old Alley. They used to be on Seminard and Robert, next to the Seminard Market. And he was on the St. Joseph night when he asked me do I want to join the P-Round band because he was leaving the band on two weeks' notice.
Oh, that's Ernest,
Paul Barbaran.
No, that was Paul Barbaran. Paul Barbaran. Paul Barbaran.
Oh, to get back to that alley, once George Lewis made some records and they called them Eclipse Alley 5, was that called Eclipse Alley or?

Well, you see, they had Maurice Durand was playing the band in the alley during them days. He had a band in there with Maurice on trumpet and it was Dodden playing banjo and you had the drum at that time was working and it was I believe I think it was I think it was Ellie Bigard or I think it was Ellie Bigard playing drum in there and doing them.
I wonder, was there really a little alley there?

It was an alley right next to the market between the market and this old Seminard Market and a place they called used to have a driver's plug next to it but it was like an alley and the bottom sat way in the rear.
Was that towards the river?

Facing like uptown. Yeah, I was at a riverside of Seminard Avenue like we call this Facing Uptown. Yeah, Facing Uptown. Yeah, that was way around well that stuff began around in the 20s too but it was during the year 1928. You know in fact before that happened we had played at a carnival party at the New Orleans Country Club with two bands it was A.J. Pirone band and John Robichaud band I was connected with John Robichaud band and they heard me play and at that same time when Paul was leaving the band I was the man it was choice for their band they liked my style of playing and they asked me to join that band and I had to go I joined that band the same year it was 1920 beginning of the month of February right after the conference season.
I was talking about Robichaud did you work with him long or
What's Robichaud? John Robichaud I worked with John Robichaud close to two years Did you? Did you work at the
lyric theater?

No I didn't play at the lyric theater when John Robichaud was happy was for the drummer during them times the fella called Red Happy I used to look at him play all the time that's way back around in 1918 and later years all through the 20s John Robichaud played during the volleyball days
How was happy? What kind of a drummer
was the style?
Happy was one of the fastest drummers I think you had in the city of New Orleans
next man next time was Zuta Singleton the jazz band Zuta Singleton we had another drummer what gave me a whole lot of ideas in the jazz band with Chris Kelly and that was Faso
Oh yes
That's the man helped me a whole lot with how to handle the snare drum
What was his name?

Faso I never knew Faso's right name I don't believe everybody knows his name Everybody knows him about Faso This year was two drums the only had was an old bass drum a snare drum and a crash cymbal no sax stands but in four cowbells and the very seldom he had a little tum-tum with it and he he was one of I think my idea was one of the best jazz drummers we had in all of us good timekeeper well that's the one I used to follow when like the first band when I used to before I even started with the Young Tuxedo band was Chris when I was just playing drum behind the piano like that in the graph and all of us one night at the old economy hall Chris was playing there and I just they made me sitting behind the drums Amelia Barnes was playing with Chris Ada Morrell on bass Lawrence Morrell on banjo Amelia Barnes on clarinet and the fellow by that name used to call Ike Williams nicknamed as Bajoon playing the trombone that's Ike Williams Chris on the trumpet that's Chris Kelly's New Orleans jazz band called the blues type band
and how was that how was that band to play with how did you enjoy it

well I was right that's what during them days we considered Chris had another one them days as one of the best blues type band in the city in New Orleans and for your best dance tempo for one tempo band was Sam Morgan band consists of six men later on he went into eight pieces with using his brother Isaiah Morgan on trumpet but Chris was a for the line of balls and lawn parties in them days Chris Kelly was rated as the best yeah for ball Chris Kelly real blues type band
well didn't he he played most of his numbers sort of slow boy

slow yeah not too fast similar like Sam Morgan band not for the high note men amongst all them fellas yeah two dangerous men's around there was Rene Kid Rene and Rick that's two high note men's amongst all them fellas but Rene he was a good executioner on his trumpet well them they called it the cornet yeah and Rick I was next to him they used to team to get lots on advertising when bands meet one another for the best and then another dangerous man we had arrived he was freakish on her was Kid Punch Kid Punch yeah but Rene still always had a top band in the line to play anything you can call in the line of jazz music understand what I mean and like I said Sam Morgan he had what you call a one standard like a real bouncy rhythm not too fast not too slow

is any of those bands you're speaking about now did you ever have occasions did they ever have occasion to have to play some music they didn't know that is to say they had to have sheets of music read from them

well some of them bands I wouldn't have seen now they when orchestration music started called the beginning some of them fellas years back in the 20's we used to call it special chorus see that'd be the second ending you know you make introduction in chorus or voice or sometimes you play the first chorus and go into voice after then you make your first ending and then you go into the second ending which is called a special chorus well we used that type music with the young tuxedo band with Bush Hall he was a pretty good reader such as little Louis Contrell the president of the musician local he was a good reader himself clandered the saxophone but you had men who couldn't read we call it them days some good spelling men you couldn't even play some of that orchestration music well the band like Pierron band them men that's all they used was stock music you see
did Chris read much

not too much of a reader I never know Chris to be too much of a reader Sam Morgan I think my idea was a better reader than Chris now Rene we all was puzzled but Rene some of the musicians I've been knowing him all my life but probably he might have been but I know he was not too much of a good reader himself to hear Rene you understand what I mean Ricard was a better reader than Rene was I'm sure he learned that while he's out in Bay St. Louis Mississippi yeah yeah Ricard did and like I said young tuxedo band that's all they played in that outfit was mostly the stock music you know orchestration and they they didn't use that kind of music much in the balls in other words in that time they gave balls around you know Saturday and Sunday nights in these bunkers on Mondays you know in the evening time like from one to six in the evening where you'd use most of the strictly head music jazz music but it was all considered jazz jazz music yeah but I mean couldn't break so
mostly late popular tunes or old blues or

mostly old blues such as the numbers they're using are like Panama Maple Leaf and High Society and this this number you call that this number here we're playing every day in our year they're using it for commercial music mostly it's the Muscat Rama all them numbers like Panama Maple Leaf High Society and we all in them days called them old Scott Joplin that's another thing that's considered as the red book this man from Scott Joplin from Chicago he had all written that music and mostly two-quote music and here people down here take it and just break it up to our way you know what I mean just swing it the jazz band and that's during the later years from when I first went in the P-Rom band that was later part of 28 and that's where we started playing at the just that weekend at the country club and later on we went to a place that's called Jack Sheen's Suburban Garden Night you know what I mean it was a trench unit's nightclub on the old Jefferson Highway and we worked out there 18 months and left from there went over to a place that's called the Suburban Garden that's on the Jefferson Highway again we worked out there it's been two years with P-Rom band then we left there we worked there all through up to the 30s and we went at the Hotel Roosevelt and worked there from January the 9th of 1932 that turned them there to call it the Venetian room and we worked there from 32 January the 9th to April the 22nd of the same year
what was that for dancing

or dinner dinner dancing dinner dancing we were waking there from 6 to 9 in the evening and go back and wait till 10 in the morning and come on the WSMB radio station every night at 12 to 1 WSMB radio station 12 to 1 broadcast one hour every night except Sundays yeah everybody said
heard that

Thursday yeah that was AJ P-Rom's dance orchestra and later all the years P-Rom braced his band up in fact he leave his band and went in to took the band band Hinojana Rania then was run by a fellow by the name was Sidney Kate playing banjo and guitar called it the Sunny South Sidney Montague on drums Sidney Kate and banjo and several other fellas I can't think of all of the names some is Wilfred on trumpet and some of Emil Fritz on saxophone that was the Sunny South obviously
did you tell us who else was in the P-Rom band when you were there I forget if you told us

was Peter Bocard still there Peter Bocard playing trumpet Henry Bocard his brother playing the bass Charlie Bocard playing the banjo Steve Lewis playing the piano Lorento Teo playing the clarinet in saxophone tenor saxophone Louis Warner playing clarinet and alto saxophone that consisted of the eight men and myself playing the drums that was AJ P-Rom eight piece dancer obviously
did they play mostly arrangements from stock arrangements or sheet from the music or did they have many head arrangements they had

a few head arrangements such as such as Mama's Gone Goodbye which was composed by Peter Bocard and a number by the name of Sister Kate and that was their own arrangements and another number about going back to Jamaica featuring Steve Lewis on the piano singing and featuring him on the piano Steve Lewis they were the only ideas about them numbers in fact Sister Kate was composed by Pierron and Clarence Williams that number was composed years ago on the street they called North Rampart and Common Pierron and William Publishing Company
yes sir I have some of their old sheet music that they published those

yeah that's right William and Pierron here left his band in 30 no it was in the later I think the early part of 33 or later part of 32 and he went and took over the Sonny South band and that's throughout the rest of Pierron and I went into Sidney Days Vien band and worked a while with them that time he had a large 10 piece orchestra around Sidney Days Vien I went and played with them
where did they play mostly
mostly field work but Sidney for before I went that outfit he traveled lots of time up and down the river on the steamer capitol
did you ever play the capitol you mentioned the other boat you played

yeah well I never made a trip with him I just played you know local engagements on the capitol such as the present but I never made a regular river trip with him all the way up the same port and I just played locally on special occasions only and I worked with that outfit and from Sidney's band when we drift around and playing stuff

different bands around the city here. And when they went into the Depression days, come in, and we were just playing, we formed a little small band with Mealy Bones, Bob Antony trumpet, Salmon, you know, his brother was there.
Who was the trumpet?

Bob Antony. Bob Antony. Anthony. I don't know him. Yeah, I think he was, he spent a while in the United States Navy with us, but he was, went into TB sickness, was in the hospital for quite a while, right after he got out of the Navy. And he, we made, we used to play down.
Is he still living?

Someone say he's living, some say he's dead. In fact, I don't know, I don't know where he's in contact. Yeah, I haven't been. Wouldn't know where to contact Bob. I haven't seen Bob in about five years. But we worked all down in Buris, and then we called a place to call it down, this place down in Seminole Parish, they call it, not Buris, Delico Island. Oh yeah. We used to work down there every Saturday night, different dances, plus local around the city, different engagements like that. Then formerly I went and worked out, and Depression come on, and I went and worked out on the WPA. First it was ERA, then the WPA. And there was forming bands at a place that called Patonis, used to be a keeper at the old parish prison, Tulane and Broad. And he had a restaurant in a dance place on Domain between Decatur and Charless, Patonis. And he had a little four piece band up there then playing nightly, which consisted of Ellie Big Ar drums and Walter Dacu playing the piano. And I think he had Charlie loved playing trumpet, if I'm not mistaken. It was a three or four piece band. And they left us used it, and they formed the ERA band. And they sent a letter on the field for me to come and join that outfit, which was sent by Louis Dumain, formed the old trumpet player, Louis Dumain.
I knew him.

Yeah, Louis Dumain. And I goes over there and had my labor card transferred from labor to musician, the old ERA band. And that's where we first started from the ERA band. We moved over to Tulane club and it's on the graphics between Roman and Bolivar.
And still where the Jolly Bunch starts out from.

Jolly Boys, that's where they have their parade starts out from. And we formally made it the WPA band. And I worked in that outfit all through the 30s, all through the 33. Clean all the way up to, way up you can say up to 1942. All that many years. Yeah. And when John and Navy band. You were talking about the WPA band again? Yeah. I went to the WPA band in November of 1933. And worked through there all through the 30s and stood with the band in which I was the last drummer in there when it comes out on the 14-piece band. And a fellow by the name of Henry Russ, Gilbert Young, two trumpet men and myself. We all joined the Navy band in the year of September the 4th, 1942 at the Custom House in New Orleans and Decadence Canal. And we left here in September the 8th. Went up to Great Lakes Illinois to take our basic training in the Navy. And we stood up there from September the 8th to August the 3rd of 1945. And we shipped down to New Orleans to Algiers. And we played over there in the Navy band from them times. Cleaned up to, let's see, August the 3rd of 1945 when I was discharged.

I remember one time, excuse me for interrupting, you were telling us how, I think it was up when you were playing at the Paddock or at the Mardi Gras, one of those two places one night. You were talking quite a while about when you played at the Navy band, you went up there and they recognized immediately that you had a different kind of a beat.

I did, yeah. I did, yeah. Well, I was, when the band used to drill out on the fields, we had lots of drummers up there from the north, didn't understand the parade music. And I made all together two bass drums, two drummers, with good orchestra drummers. And I learned them how to play the bass drum in parade style. They already know the music for dance band, but they didn't understand the New Orleans style. And our band, the place of taking the 8th week training up there, we stood up there 3 months and 21 days. Because our chief was still down here, the custom house, Chief Cooper. And we had to stay up there and just, after our boot training was over in 8 weeks, we'd just lay around there and play all the graduation exercises and all the inspections on Saturdays.

Can you pin down and tell us what is the difference between the New Orleans beat and the other, can you explain any of that? Well I wouldn't know that. I didn't know that. Can you explain any of that?

Yes, it's a single beat you had, a steady single beat you had on a bass drum, you know, playing these different styles of marches. But they raid our whole band in New Orleans, in Great Lakes, when we was formerly, a band consisted of 23 men and one with the chief make 24. When we break it down to 15 or 16-piece dance obviously, we didn't have no special arrangement during the training time, so we played stock music in the training camp. And they considered it mostly like New Orleans style with the attack. Other members of the naval, I mean musicians of the naval barracks, they considered it as New Orleans style. That's the way they did it, they considered it, you understand? And then when we played, one day I was told, doing a graduation exercise when it was all over, I was greeted by some of the sailors with the nice tempo I had on the bass drum. I was playing bass drum at that time with the Navy band. And they agreed on the tempo I had. And that's why, from that day on, I was asked by two other good top drummers about how to make them attacks, you understand? But learning, because they were puzzling, come down to playing that two-fold and six-eighth music, which I still said it was good to orchestra drum, but that had them kind of puzzled. Well, we already had it through playing the funeral bands and prayers and around, we already knew that, you know, commit that to memories. You didn't worry about the music too much, but you can feel it. You can almost feel them marches, you know, through playing, especially the drummer. And that's why I said it in our instrument. We had another fellow who died recently by the name of Booker, Washington, we always would call him Booker, bass player. He learned lots of fellows up there how to play the bass on too for parade bands and different marching bands like that, Booker. And he, when we got down to Al Jays, he's a fellow by the name of playing some of these rock and roll artists called Frank Field. He learned him how to play the bass. Yeah, he's Frank Field. He used to come down here with George Williams, piano player, which was the leader of the Navy band, assistant leader you could say, piano player. Well, he's played all of this in the piano, George Williams, trumpet, saxophone and piano. And he arranged, put in this, Claiborne Williams' oldest son.
I was going to say he was Claiborne, I was going to ask if he was...

Claiborne Williams, from Napoleonville, Louisiana. Claiborne Williams' oldest son. That's George Williams. Well, he arranged and he made first class rake in the Navy band. And he did all the arrangements for the Navy band. Him and a fellow by the name of Boyt Traynor Adams from Tyler, Texas. There's two arrangements. But George was in charge of the band, George Williams.
Harold Dejean was in one of those bands.

Harold Dejean was in our same unit. Harold Dejean. Gilbert Jung, Henry Russ. That's all the fellas from this. That's the two men that we all joined together, was Henry Russ and Gilbert Jung. We all joined the Navy, the Navy band the same day. And from that time on, well, we just got out of the Navy. I'm trying to think now. I came back in the field and played several... did some funeral work with Peter Bocca and them. I think at that time it was called the brass band. It was considered the onward, part of the onward brass band. I might have the name wrong, but I think...
After the war?
Right after the war, yeah, after I got out of the Navy.
When did you get out of the Navy?
In August the 3rd of 1945. 1945.
I remember about the first time that I remember meeting you and hearing you is when we made those records with Wooden Joe over the...
Yeah, well I was in the Navy then. That's the night I was around in 44, wasn't it?
No, 45. May.
May of 45. May of 45. When I got out that same year.

And the Navy Dodds was supposed to be there. Be there, yeah. He had his arm or something so they got me there. Yeah, he got me that last minute to come and record. Still had on your uniform, I remember.

Yeah, yeah, it was a night at the old artesian hall, called the Night in New Orleans. I made a recording that night. It was Wooden Joe, they weren't there playing... Yes, Wooden Joe and Burbank and Lawrence. Lawrence and we had Boots playing trombones, playing the bass. Jim Crow playing the trombone. That's right. The night we made it recorded.
And you got out of the Navy then just a few months after that in August.
After that, August in 45, yeah, the show out of the Navy.
Did they still have some of the old onward band at that time? I didn't know they called it that.

Well, that's what I'm thinking now. I placed several parades and funerals with it, but I know it was led by Peter Boccoff over in Algiers. I played lots of funerals with them on that. I think it was called the Onward Brass Band, part of it. Peter might explain it more better.
Yeah, I don't remember that he told us about that particular group.

Yeah, yeah. I'm trying to think now. Who would I want in with after that? We played around here, 45 and let's see. I was doing field work then and working doing Days of Work. And I think in the year of 1950, Johnny Papacelestand's Jazz Band. I worked in there from 50 to 52. The 90s of Papacelestand, New Orleans Jazz Band. I played with him. When I left in that outfit, we went. Then I started working different field work with Poissy Humphrey. And then we started playing and we formally took that outfit and went into Sweet Emma's Band. Between Poissy and Emma, we worked that outfit.
How many years have you been with Emma now?

We've been six years now. Six years. Yeah, because we first, Emma played a while with us at Sid DeVilla's place on Boybent Street with Kit Howard, part of George Lewis Band. When they made a tour to Chicago. And we played near a while with the band. And we worked near, I think it was about two months or maybe longer. And we'd come on out there and that's where Emma and Poissy kept the band up. Then Emma got the title of Sweet Emma, you see. And she fixed it. She fixed it.
When did she start? We haven't interviewed her yet. We'll try to get her in a week or so now. Yeah. When did she start using those bells? Do you remember?

That idea was given to Emma by Miss Valenti at the paddock. Emma had a tendency to play in the piano and pat her foot like you're using, you know, drum motion, the left and right foot. And Miss Valenti first gave her the idea to take the bells and put around your ankle to crack the people's attention. Miss Valenti gave her the first idea how to do that.
One time I was going to ask you, Said, and that was about your grandparents. Did they, we never asked you, did they play any musical instruments?
My grandparents, I couldn't remember. My grandparents, because they are, I don't know.
The family seemed so musical. Musical, yeah. I wondered if it came to him for it.

Well, I don't know what's on the phrase. My father was honest when I was, no, well wait now, Salmon's daddy, Lawrence's daddy was Billy Moran, he was the number one bass player. Yeah. Yeah, he played with the old time superior band. That consists of Peter Bocaught playing trumpet and violin. And I think there's Walter Brunnen, I can't remember all the men's them days, that's way back. He called it the superior band.
We have a picture of that old band. That band, yeah. Well that's Peter Bocaught. Walter Brunnen, I believe, on drums.
Walter Brunnen on drums.
And Bunk was playing cornett.
Oh, them the men's, that's right. That's the old time superior band.
Did you ever play with Bunk? I guess not the old days.

Not the old days. I played with Bunk, yeah. And after he, George and I came back from New York. That was another thing I forgot right after the wall, I was playing with that outfit, you know, different spot jobs, yeah, with Bunk and George and them. And I made that trip that time with George to California, remember? Oh yeah. That was in 56. George went replacing Joe Boston, the drummer. Well I played up there with them and came on back.
Did you ever enjoy joining Earl Hines?

Earl Hines, man, you sure did, yeah. They was working at the Hangover Club in San Francisco. Yeah. And we did two weeks up there and then we come down to L.A. and they had three months, but I didn't stay. I came on back and Joe was released off his job and I placed him back with the band. Yeah. I came back down, yeah, and I've been playing ever since. That's where I joined the outfit with Kid Howard and them at City Village Place. Yeah. And from there we went over to Poesie Hunt and Emma. I've been playing with them ever since. Yeah, present.

That covers, I think most of your jobs pretty well. We might talk for a few minutes we have left. Yeah. But you can remember anything else about your father and the type of music he played or any early bands he might have played in?

No, I just know him as playing, he played guitar, the years when we was all small. And I do know from music he was a mattress maker and he was a Baptist minister. Oh, he's a minister. A minister, Baptist minister, yes. But now whatever, I wouldn't know any bands he ever played with way back before my childhood.
I wondered if he played in any bands or just…

Yeah, that part I wouldn't know. Did your mother sing or play? My mother was the number one singer. Now she was a good entertainer at the church from a little girl at Thompson and Me Chapel. Used to be on Send Rock and… Was that Methodist?
Methodist Church, yeah.
Your father was…
He was Baptist, my mother was Methodist.

Oh, that's right. Yeah. And she sang from a little girl who played concerts and sang in the church. In fact, she sang it to the church in her later years until she died under the… A scholar by the name of Lewis Nelson played trombone. His mother and father, his father used to be a bass songster in the church chorus and his mother was an organist. It was the doctor, Nelson. Yeah, Dr. Nelson and Mrs. Nelson playing the organ.
I knew she played piano in the… Yeah, I knew that. He told me about that.
That's the chorus they sang with. Yeah.
The same church.
Same church, Thompson and Me Chapel, St. Rock and St. Claude. And that's all my family I know, the musicals. Were there very much stuff there with stuff

My brother was a drummer way before my time, you know, and I come right behind him. That was way back in 1919 and 1920. He played with different bands around here like Lewis, you know, and Kid René and all of them. And I just took the style behind him, pick it up behind him. He gave it up in the late 20s. Sam, he gave it up, yeah.
Did you ever try to play on his drums when you were in the middle?

I played a while on his drums because I didn't have any drums during them days. I used to use his drums like around the house and sometimes little small parties, you know, with a piano and drums. He told me when he wouldn't be using them. I'd use them sometimes. And like I said, I sent off to a music publisher in the house in the Willis and Music people and bought my first snare drum. And I bought my bass drum local.

I'm going to ask you, how you, how the drummer, what's the drummer's part in the New Orleans band, Saeed? Where in the first place do you get your beat from? How do you know the tempo that any number's going to be in?

The leaders explain it to you. Sometimes a man just pat his foot. Anybody leading a, could be a piano player. Sometimes they just pick up like that. Without telling you anything, you know, just like our outfit right now. Sometimes we just pick up. You just fall right in behind him. Some leaders have stomped their foot. If a man playing the sax or trumpet, he might tell you. Then sometimes, some numbers you're so familiar playing. If you just know the tempo, they're going to always play. Then you see, if it's going to be a fast or slow number. And sometimes, before that, some guys might stomp and give you four beats with his patty's foot like that. You know, he stomp it and then you just give you the tempo. And you pick it up. And the drummer just fall right in. Sometimes if you want to hit together, you just can manage. He might just stomp his foot off twice. Maybe he'll just say one, just make two pats on the floor. And you can hear that. You're going right and hit together then. Sometimes you just sneak right on in there. Just pick up a number. You're just falling right together. Many times, like my little outfit, I just watch them. Sometimes they go to pick up a number. I just attack with them right off the reel.
I heard it Saturday night.

Yeah. Yeah. We just attack. But I tell you, I know the number. Now, sometimes they tell you, they're going to tell you what number. They're going to tell you what number. A proportional request of the number. Or sometime before, years ago. And sometimes they do. The trumpet player announce what number he's going to play. Make a ball tune on his horn, you see. Then if it's going to be panamo, we know we play that not too slow. And sometimes kind of fast. Well, when he just said panamo, if he hit two beats, or if he just pick it up with the horn, we fall right in there. You know his tempo. And if it's a slow number, like St. Louis Blues, where we don't play that too fast. Well, sometimes he stomp that number or give it two beats. And you pick that right up, you know, your tempo. Well, it's different than brass bands. Well, you all know how brass bands start. The drummer bring them in on that. Yeah. Yeah. That's all. They have to snap it up, make his cadence, and he make it, change his different beats, and go into like a march or something, and then he bring the band in, you see. With the three beats on your bass drum. Military band is kind of a little different from that, because you make, you play a regular cadence like that, and then you might make a double rap or a roll, and then the bass drum might hit one beat and bring you in. Yeah. Yeah. It's going to be a military band, because you have a drum major up ahead there. He's giving you the tempo with his bat tone, you understand? Yeah. But I mean, our way of playing around here with the old brass bands, like funeral band, after you're playing, you've got your muffled snare drum, you'll slow your tempos, the slowest, we'll call it old time, fofo tempo, slow it, and the snare drummer, his dyes tempo down, and the bass drum players, the man, bring them in with three slow beats. He's a little...
Imagine a playing drum in an Orleans brass band must be more difficult than playing it in a military band.

It's more difficult. It's much harder. It's much harder, because first of all, the puzzle is the average musician that's getting off on their left feet. On your left, your left step out, you see. If you get that bass drum on that left, start off like that, everybody will be on time.
It's a bass drum on the left.

On the left, always take your bass drum on your left beat. If your band, if the snare drum is this diadon slow, if he's giving you the cadence, and if you're getting ready to play a funeral march, he just bring his drum down to a slow tempo or into a light roll, and the bass drum player might holler, watch me. That's the way Trapani used to do it, watch me. And everybody be waiting, and he just take the bass drum and hit three slow beats, not too far apart, you understand? And then after that third beat, them horns will pick up. They'll come right on in there, whether they're playing, if they've got music for their parts or not, they'll come right on in on time.
That's for the dirge, for the dirges, or are they...
No, that's for the funeral marches.
Yeah, the real slow marches.
Real slow funeral marches, yeah, real slow marches. They make tree, they give you the tree beats on the bass drum.
Did you enjoy playing the snare drum or bass drum?

Well, I used to like both of them when I was a much younger man. I used to, I played lots of time, I used to alternate with George Williams' brass band. We'd be playing the Jolly Boys parade and different parades around here. I used to alternate with George, get tired, he gave me the bass, but I used to like both of them. Yeah, those times it's by Gitman now, he's toting that bass drum because I used to suffer with my spine, you know. I had a fall in the Navy there, and it injured my left spine there, and that weight kind of hurts me. So that's why I was hospitalized in 43. I stood six months in the Naval Hospital for that treatment. I can't hear it too heavy on my left shoulder, no, it worries my back, boy. So that's what gets taken out of time. The smaller somebody in the Bayes drum, no, it may be, but the length of time, it is aggro, it kind of worries me, you know, right in this back here. So that's why sometimes I stick to the snare drum. But I used to like to play both of them, based on the snare drum.
In the orchestra, is there anything else you can tell about the way you think of your drums? Is it mainly as a timekeeper to fill in, or what do you think of your...

Well, I think a drum, yeah. That's a part to you. I figured a drum is mostly a timekeeping instrument. It's strictly a time instrument, you know what I mean? And you just feel your own ideas, how they, you know, different numbers. You play, you understand the feeling. I think in the line of playing jazz music, you've managed to use plenty of snare drums. In less cymbal way. Yeah, it's a day all these young kids always playing cymbals. Yeah, a snare drum feels a band move. In a line of small bands, it really feels move, a snare drum. And years ago, we played mostly snare drums. And make your bells and your chonny in between breaks, and use your cry cymbals going out. Open them or you choke them. Going out, you see. And when they come out, first with the overhead socks, then first they had the flow sock cymbals. That didn't last a lot. We used to call them flow beaters. But that didn't last, and they went over to, people called them the hi-hat cymbals. We called them sock cymbals. Sometimes a man might play that choke that, you know, on his drums. You know, to play it nice and soft. A person's singing or something like that. Some guys might use a stick and one wire brush. Different ideas. It's just different ideas of different drummers, yeah. Now I adopt the idea of playing with my cymbal, choke, and this play light on the two sticks, and the public took to that. They like it. Yeah, I started that idea. I started that idea, my own idea. And people took to that. Some liked to hear me play on the Chinese block with one stick and just play on the cymbal. Because they tell me they do that. At the old Absinthe House. They like that, you know. And just play Chinese block with like a little light rhythm on there, you know. And just take one hand, the left hand, and just beat on the cymbal, tap that light, and they get kicks out of that. That was my idea. They just took to that. Some wanted to play some number all the way through on the bell. There's one car bell. Yeah.
When did drum solos first come in? I noticed, of course, today you have to play drum solos over there at times.
Most of the times, yeah.
But when did that start, do you think?

Oh, I wouldn't know how that's. Well, the old-time drummers, no, they didn't take a whole solo. I don't remember none of them taking a whole, but they took breaks. Make a break on the ending. In some numbers, them days you might have some numbers called for a four-bar break, a drummer running there. But most of the endings of the drummer are running there. Now, all those men I know used to take plenty of drum solos. I was doing a flash when they were redhead happy when he's worked at the old Lyric, Lyric Theater. He'd take plenty of drum solos. And that was only with Carl Bells. He had one shiny block. No sock stand to do show, but he was very flashy. And Faso was another man. But I asked, like the drummers doing it today, taking chorus, you know, one or two choruses. I don't remember drummers doing that all the time. I don't remember. Because we didn't do it in my time of playing, you know, all the way a chorus all the way through. Maybe some of them did it, but I never see any of them, you know.
People have told me that one of the main things about New Orleans drummers in a dance band, they use a little more bass drum and keep that bass drum moving out.
Yes.
Did you ever notice out of other drummers from away from here that they don't use as much bass?

They don't, no. I mean, I've seen drummers play it with big bands. They hardly test the band. I've seen guys play this, take their foot and tip their foot pedal, and just keep their beat against the drum. But they'd be playing a whole lot of these cymbals. Yeah, I've seen that. Yeah, but they'd be fast, a whole lot of parallelism on their snare drum. Another thing we were short around, lots of drummers couldn't roll much around here. Roll a snare drum, you see, they couldn't do that. That was no entouphal in time. All the old drummers, mostly, would roll a snare drum.
Did you ever have any lessons later on? You mentioned you'd like a snare drum.

I mentioned what, I had some ideas in line. The first man gave me ideas about getting those old, Leonard Bishy, the old dentist. He was a dentist and formed me a trombone player, but he didn't keep it as a profession. He played it as a sideline. Old Doc Bishy, yeah. He bought a method for me himself, from Philip Woylein Music still. And I used to get to come up with a man, Louis Contrell, sometimes, to give me different pointers about it. And working with different bands, guys help you out, you understand how it was?
Which method did that rise?

That was a Carl Fisher. Carl Fisher. Carl Fisher method, that's right. The old drum method. The old Carl Fisher method. The old stuff stuff One who used to give me ideas about different divisions of music was Bush Hall, trumpet player, like I tell you, we played with the Young Tuxedo Band. And he gave me different pointers about dividing different music. And then I studied my own self, you understand, take the methods and self-practice and just get the ideas, just come to you, listen to other bands play. Then when the swing band was famous, well that gave me more pointers too, listen to them on the radio. It's just like in Georgia, hearing them big bands playing, them guys executing on them instruments, you see. That helped you out a whole lot too.
When you were young, did you practice very much by yourself on the drums?

Lots of times, lots of times. After I started playing with bands, I used to practice many days. I was living on 17, 18 on Village Street. And many times I'd ring up my drums by myself, we call it front drum, you know, just practice on myself.
Well I forgot to ask about your family, what part of town were they, did they live in?

Of all our life, that's easy, I was born 1123 Two Row Street. That's between Murray and St. Claude. Left from there we went in the next block, 1223 Two Row Street. And I stood there until I got married, January 31st, 1923.
Did most of the Mareros and Barnes and all of them live around that neighborhood too?

The Mareros lived on, in the 1100 block, I was, we was 23, there was 25, the Mareros lived next to them. John, Salmon, that's when their father was living, Billy Moran. And the Barnes at that time was living, let's see now, the Barnes at that time was living on, I believe on Spain and Ville. Yeah, my old aunt Katrine, that's Milla's mother.
But all downtown in that... All downtown in that...

All downtown. Never did go otherwise out to the 7th or the 8th Ward. Just living that bondage between the 7th and the 8th Ward. All of our lives, from the 7th Ward to the 8th Ward. One time the Mareros was living back on Maroney Street between Johnson and Galvis. Another time the bonds was living on Maroney and Oikwalt, that's the 8th Ward. And the Mareros was living on Spain between Ville and that was the 8th, that consisted of the 8th Ward. Yeah. Me, I was living all my days in the 7th Ward. Never was out of it. From Two Row Street to the boundary of Seminard, Ville, around the old alley. I lived in that neighborhood for years and years. Seminard between Ville and Robinson. And that's the funniest I ever lived back where we're living right now. But I always lived in the 7th Ward.
We were talking about your practicing and I interrupted you. Did you ever practice on drum pads or always on your...

Never practiced on a drum pad in my life. Never did practice on a drum. I used to practice on a drum. I used to practice on a drum. Tables. I've seen drum pads in later years, you know, at different music stores, but I didn't know what that looked like years ago. Oh, I guess so. It used to take sticks or two forks or sometimes beat on a kitchen table. Oh, years ago, like I first said, when we had the old time on Two Row Street, they had a band used to call Ted Lewis, had a record they called Patchy. Oh, yes.
I remember that.

Very tinnish. Those records, you know, it was like the recording today and I used to like to play that all the time, Ted Lewis Jazz Band. And I used to play that record over and over on our graph and over. And just take two sticks, my brother, two sticks and beat against the wall with that front, if you understand. And just call myself falling behind, patting my foot on the floor. And that's why I just play that record over in the evening time around the house like that. Just play that over in Patchy's, Ted Lewis Band.
I was going to ask if you like heavy sticks or light sticks?
I like sticks, no, sort of a medium size, yeah, for dance band, medium size. Not too heavy, not too light.
And what about the bass drum? Do you like a bigger bass drum or smaller or the tone doesn't make much difference in the tone?

My idea, the bass drum I'm working on now is a 1426. And I had that drum now since 1950 I've got that drum. And it's, I think it's, my idea about it is it's got a better tone than a smaller size bass, you know, for a lot of jazz band. But I don't know, I can't take it to the smaller size bass, you know, the modern style.
I don't like it, it looks like a little tom-tom.

Little tom-toms, yeah. Really? But I really like the bass drum I'm working on now. I think that's a 1426 bass. And I believe that's, my idea is best for jazz, better volume. And then you take this kind of damp weather right now, that instrument will still, you just give it a certain tune-up, it'll hold its volume, you know. And the way I pad, man, mute it. Now I just have a side muffler to it, and I take some old pieces of these, what you call this, these pads you put on your back, you know, for pains like that, these plastic pads. And I make that in a round shape, I figure it's the biggest ashtray, for the ball to hit it, get it. And I notice that gives it a better tone in my mute. You see, some guys mute the drummer, but I just, I don't ever mute my, I was learned, it was told by old drummers, when they first started muting drums, don't mute the back part of a drum, always mute the side where your ball hit it. Some guys used to use it.

a piece of rag over it, well that makes the drum too tudd like, you understand? It's like your snare. Now the good drum like Contra, they all explain it, tune your snare drum, maybe a twist more on the batter side and let the snare side a little looser. It gives it a better volume too.
Do you try to tune up your drums to any certain pitch like on the piano or on another

instrument? I did it years ago, tried to reach it, yeah, years ago I used to do it when I worked with Pilon band and we tried it, we did it awhile, you know. Sometimes it'll hold up, sometimes it wouldn't. Sometimes the weather, the way a drum will, see like you get into a heated place like in the wintertime, the drum with the heat, you understand it'll draw off the head, you can sometimes pop it. Or you might get a rain, you take the summer night, you can have winter weather, you get a rain like out there now, that could interfere with the snare drum most of the time too. That'll give you trouble around this part of the world.
Have much trouble breaking heads on your snare drum ever?

Not too much, no. Last drum head I had broke was the Sunday we played, I played with the Eureka Brass Band, we had a rain and I was a drummer, yeah, couldn't help that Sunday, that's quite a while back, head broke on me.
Did it get soft and your stick went through it or?

No, it just rim cut, in fact I was covering it all the time, you know, this wiping, we were making different little stops. But before the parade was over there, she rim cut on me from the dampness, you see. And I had to unwind it, in fact she just had it there, couldn't do nothing with it, because you tried to play it, you couldn't sound like nothing, you see. But we just had to finish the parade, and the band, when the drums get wet, they don't look, you know the band, they expect to hear those drums, they know they don't sound like nothing, you can't play it. Now they did, they tell me they got covers to put on the drum.
They say you ought to try to sell those plastic covers.
That's what they tell me, they tell me they got all that now.
You can get a piece of plastic back from the cleaners, from, you know, in the way I had.
Yeah, that would take it, yeah.
Something like that would help.
Help it a whole lot, help a snare drum out, yeah.
Well, there's about another minute here, I was going to ask if there's any of the other old-time drummers, anything you could add about, say, old man Cantrell, or anybody else?

Well, you see, all of them I know is like I told you, a fellow of you know, he always talk about Black Benny, I never know Benny's right name, but you know Happy. You know Happy, you know, Ernest Rapania, we call it Trap, Faisal, Willigan, I forgot to mention him, that's all, and Alfred William, you know all of them. Yes. Chani, I forgot who that's about him.
We interviewed him a few months ago.

Chani, now that's the original drummer from the Tuxedo Band, that's the original drummer. Chani Bebe, because of his right name, his right name, I mean his nickname, we call his right name, Abbie William.
There were a few of the other drummers uptown, you remember a fellow by the name of Henry Zeno.
Henry Zeno, I forgot all about him, I'm glad you mentioned him, Henry Zeno, yeah. Then we had Red, Red Duga. Yes, I never knew Henry.
Yeah, you heard of Red Duga.
Let me see, Henry Zeno, I forgot, that's Parade Man and a dance man. Henry Zeno. Henry Martin, is that the name?
Henry Martin.
How was he?
A good drummer?

Good drummer, good drummer. He played a while, before you run out, when we, Pierron Brookerby's old band, and they formed a band, they called it the Creole Serenade, with Peter Volcar and Dwight Newman and Charlie and Henry, they had six pieces, Henry Zeno was their drummer. I forgot about that.
Or Martin or Zeno.
Huh?
Martin or Zeno.
Some call him Henry Martin, some say Henry Zeno, but he's right name, Henry Martin.
I thought they were two different fellas, but did they not?
No, no, Henry Martin, that's right, Henry Martin, you know, slim, bronziker looking fella, yeah, I forgot about him. Always smoked sigils. Then you had, uh, I met their mother once, uh,
Yeah. Kept the school, she was the caretaker of a school up there.
Yeah.
On Perdido Street.

Now we had another drummer too now, we call him Joe, uh, a little short fella, he's another parade man, I forgot about him too, it was Joe, uh, I forgot the guy's name, uh, oh, you know, I can't hear that man's name if he needed. He was another drummer, I forgot from uptown there. He was, his name was Joe Sutton, uh,
He was good on bass drum or snare drum?

He was good on both, but he mostly played with snare drum. He was, uh, I thought it was short fella. His name was Joe, uh, Joe, uh, not Joe Watkins. Somebody else will probably tell us about him. Yeah, yeah, I can't think of that man's last, cause you want his right name.
Like Joe Watkins when we were talking to him, he came up with the fella that Bunk used to talk about two bits and then nobody knew his name. Do you remember two bits ever? No.
Two bits.
Did he have a nickname, this, uh, Joe you're singing on?
No, uh, he was, oh, that fella's name, I know he's got this, it was, it sounded like a Watkins, but it's not what he's right name.
Not a Watson, was it?
No, uh, Joe Watkins or Watson, something like that. I think it's similar to that.
Yeah, well, we're just about out of the tape now, unless there's something else that you can think of.

Yeah, well, I'm trying to think now of all them old drummers. I mentioned, uh, yeah, I mentioned Red Dugal. Yes. And, uh, you know Henry Russ played drum too, eh? Little Trump, little Henry Russ played trumpet. Oh, I never heard of him. He played drum too, yeah, Henry Russ. He used to live uptown too, he's not an old drummer. Yeah, that's the end of it here.
Thank you.

segments.title: Opening and Frazier's birth date
segments.summary: Russell opens the interview at Frazier's home, 14 December 1960; Frazier gives his birth date as 23 February 1904.

segments.title: Name and the nickname Cie
segments.summary: Frazier spells his name and explains the Creole-derived nickname Cie, used since school days.

segments.title: Fraser family ties to the Barnes and Morrell musicians
segments.summary: He explains that the Barnes and Morrell musicians' mothers were his father's Fraser sisters.

segments.title: Father's guitar, mattress making, and brother Sam the drummer
segments.summary: His father played guitar and made mattresses; oldest brother Sam was a drummer who no longer plays.

segments.title: Brothers, cousins and aunts and uncles in the Fraser family
segments.summary: He names his other brothers, piano-playing cousins and his father's siblings.

segments.title: Learning drums on Sam's drums and a Victrola
segments.summary: He picked up drums practicing on sticks, Victrola records and Sam's drums, with no lessons.

segments.title: First bands: Golden Rule band, Young Tuxedo Band lineup
segments.summary: He lists his first band's members and its change into the Young Tuxedo Band with its personnel.

segments.title: First drum set, cowbells, pedals and the Idlewild boat
segments.summary: He describes his first Ludwig bass drum, Leedy-type snare, cowbells and pedals, and the switch to floor pedals in 1927 on the Idlewild.

segments.title: Young Tuxedo Band jobs, leader and pay
segments.summary: The band played country clubs and society dances; Bush Hall led it, and he describes the pay rates.

segments.title: Joining the musicians' union and Don Albert
segments.summary: He recalls joining the union around 1928, Tats Alexander, and the band passing to Dwight Newman and Don Albert.

segments.title: Young Tuxedo as a dance band versus brass bands; Ernest Rapanya
segments.summary: The Young Tuxedo was strictly a dance band; Rapanya started Frazier in brass band work.

segments.title: Ernest Rapanya's career and duplex snare drum
segments.summary: He describes Rapanya as a cabaret drummer and his aluminum duplex snare, now used by Alfred Williams.

segments.title: Joining Piron's band after Paul Barbarin, and the alley
segments.summary: Barbarin's departure from Piron's band opened the job for Frazier; talk of Robichaux and an alley bar.

segments.title: Working with John Robichaux
segments.summary: He worked close to two years with John Robichaux and recalls Red Happy at the Lyric Theater.

segments.title: Drummers Happy and Faso, and Chris Kelly and Sam Morgan bands
segments.summary: He praises Happy and Faso, then recalls playing with Chris Kelly's band and compares it with Sam Morgan's.

segments.title: Reading music versus head arrangements; repertoire
segments.summary: He discusses which bandleaders read music, stock music versus head jazz, and repertoire like Panama and High Society.

segments.title: Piron band engagements and the Roosevelt Hotel broadcasts
segments.summary: Piron's band played country clubs and Jefferson Highway nightclubs, then the Roosevelt in 1932 with a WSMB broadcast.

segments.title: Piron band personnel and repertoire
segments.summary: He lists the men in Piron's eight-piece band and its few head arrangements, and Piron leaving in 1932-33.

segments.title: Sidney Desvigne's band and the steamer Capitol
segments.summary: He worked with Desvigne's ten-piece band and played local dates on the steamer Capitol.

segments.title: Small Depression band with Bob Anthony
segments.summary: During the Depression he formed a small band that worked Delacroix Island dances.

segments.title: ERA and WPA bands
segments.summary: He joined the ERA band, later the WPA band, working in it from 1933 until 1942.

segments.title: Navy band at Great Lakes and the New Orleans beat
segments.summary: He joined the Navy band in 1942 and taught Northern drummers parade-style bass drum; he describes George Williams and the band.

segments.title: Wooden Joe recording of 1945 and brass band after discharge
segments.summary: He recorded with Wooden Joe in May 1945, left the Navy in August, and played funerals with Bocage's band.

segments.title: Papa Celestin, Poesie Humphrey and Sweet Emma's band
segments.summary: He worked with Papa Celestin 1950-52, then Humphrey and Sweet Emma, and tells how Emma got her ankle bells.

segments.title: Grandparents and Billy Marrero in the Superior band
segments.summary: Asked about family musicians, he recalls Billy Marrero in the old Superior Band.

segments.title: Playing with Bunk, George Lewis and Earl Hines in 1956
segments.summary: He played with Bunk and George Lewis, toured California in 1956 and played with Earl Hines in San Francisco.

segments.title: Parents' music: father's ministry and mother's church singing
segments.summary: He describes his father as a Baptist minister and his mother as a church singer.

segments.title: Brother Sam's drums as his model
segments.summary: He followed his brother Sam's style and used Sam's drums until he bought his own.

segments.title: How the drummer sets tempo in dance and brass bands
segments.summary: He explains how tempo is set in dance bands and how bass drum cadences bring in brass bands and funerals.

segments.title: Snare versus bass drum and his back injury
segments.summary: He liked both drums but injured his spine in the Navy and now prefers snare.

segments.title: Drumming as timekeeping and his cymbal style
segments.summary: He thinks of drums as timekeeping, favors snare, and describes his own light cymbal and Chinese block ideas.

segments.title: Drum solos and the New Orleans bass drum
segments.summary: He says old drummers took breaks, not choruses, and New Orleans drummers used more bass drum and rolls.

segments.title: Learning drums: Doc Bechet, method book and practice
segments.summary: He learned from Doc Bechet's method, Louis Cottrell and Bush Hall, and practiced alone.

segments.title: Where the family lived in the Seventh Ward
segments.summary: He gives the addresses where he and his Marrero and Barnes relatives lived downtown.

segments.title: Practicing on tables and the Ted Lewis record
segments.summary: As a boy he practiced on tables and played along with a Ted Lewis record.

segments.title: Sticks, bass drum size, muting and tuning, drumheads
segments.summary: He gives views on sticks, his 14x26 bass drum, muting, tuning, weather, and a broken head at a parade.

segments.title: Other old-time drummers and the original Tuxedo drummer
segments.summary: Asked about other drummers, he lists several and says Chaney was the original Tuxedo drummer.

segments.title: Henry Zeno and Henry Martin
segments.summary: He and Russell discuss the drummer Henry Zeno, whom he says is really Henry Martin.

segments.title: An uptown parade drummer named Joe whose surname he cannot recall
segments.summary: He tries to recall the surname of a short uptown drummer named Joe.

segments.title: Closing remarks at end of tape
segments.summary: Near the end of the tape he adds Red Dugal and Henry Russ and the interview ends.
